traveler: Simonides of Ceos (Simonides son of Leoprepes)
stop_name: Ioulis, Ceos, born to Leoprepes
date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Suda (sigma 439) gives the 56th Olympiad, 556/552 BCE, and adds in the same sentence that some have written the 62nd, 532/528, a variant it neither resolves nor prefers. The conventional 556 is arrived at by counting back from the Parian Marble's death notice of 468/467 at the age of ninety; the Suda itself says eighty-nine, one short. The birthplace, Ioulis on Ceos, is uncontested across the testimonia. The father's name Leoprepes is attested in the patronymic used by Herodotus, by the Parian Marble, and by the epitaph Callimachus quotes.

traveler: Simonides of Ceos (Simonides son of Leoprepes)
stop_name: Karthaia, the chorus drilled above the sea
date_confidence: Tradition, not documented. No contemporary source places Simonides at Karthaia or names him a chorus trainer there; the association is a later inference from his profession and from Ceos's known choral culture, transmitted through the Suda and repeated in modern synthesis (J. H. Molyneux, Simonides: A Historical Study, 1992). The site itself is securely identified and excavated: the temples of Apollo and Athena on the southeastern coast of Kea. The date given here orders the segment only.

traveler: Simonides of Ceos (Simonides son of Leoprepes)
stop_name: Delos, the Cean delegation before Apollo
date_confidence: Reconstruction, offered as context rather than as an attested visit. Cean participation in the Delian festival of Apollo is documented in Cycladic epigraphy and in the Delian hymn tradition; no Simonidean text and no ancient testimonium places Simonides himself on Delos. Included because it is the circuit a Cean chorus master works, and flagged as unattested for him personally.

traveler: Simonides of Ceos (Simonides son of Leoprepes)
stop_name: Athens, brought to the city by Hipparchus
date_confidence: Attested for the invitation, reconstructed for the date. Aristotle (or pseudo-Aristotle), Constitution of the Athenians 18, and pseudo-Plato, Hipparchus 228b-c, both say Hipparchus drew Simonides to Athens alongside Anacreon; neither gives a year, and the round age of thirty is a later biographical convenience. The pseudo-Platonic dialogue is not by Plato and is itself a defence of the Peisistratids, so its picture of a cultured Hipparchus is interested testimony.

traveler: Simonides of Ceos (Simonides son of Leoprepes)

Pol. 18 or pseudo-Plato's Hipparchus, neither of which mentions Lasus. No contest, year, or chorus is preserved. The date orders the segment.

traveler: Simonides of Ceos (Simonides son of Leoprepes)

No date within Simonides' life is preserved for it, and no poem of his mentions the episode. The date given here orders the Thessalian segment and is not evidence.

traveler: Simonides of Ceos (Simonides son of Leoprepes)

stop_name: Crannon, the roof comes down
date_confidence: Reconstruction, and disputed in antiquity itself. Cicero, De Oratore 2.353-354, is the earliest full account. Quintilian, Inst. Or. 11.2.11-17, writing about 95 CE, calls the rescue by the two youths 'purely fictitious' on the ground that Simonides nowhere mentions so flattering a miracle, and reports that ancient authorities disagreed over both the victim and the town. The Rhetorica ad Herennium 3.16-24, earlier than Cicero, expounds the loci-and-images method in full and names no inventor and tells no story. Pliny, Natural History 7.24, credits Simonides with the invention and gives no banquet.

Quintilian notes only that Cicero's version 'gained wider circulation'. Both pins are given because antiquity gave both.
